fields.security_summary: HBM3 is a DRAM memory standard; it provides no confidentiality (encryption), authentication, or access control at the protocol layer — stored data is plaintext. Its security-adjacent features are reliability/integrity mechanisms: on-die ECC, link ECC, command/address parity, RAS error reporting, soft-repair, and refresh management (RFM) bounding row-hammer-class disturbance.

security_features_at_protocol_level.purpose: Detect/correct array errors transparently; integrity, not confidentiality.
Protect data on the channel against transmission errors.
Detect corruption of commands/addresses on the R/C buses.
Bound row-hammer-class disturbance, mitigating a known DRAM fault-injection class.
Map out failing cells for reliability; not an access-control feature.
Surface uncorrectable/severe errors to the host for serviceability.

fields.no_confidentiality: No on-die encryption of stored data; payload is plaintext. Memory encryption is implemented by the host SoC, not by HBM3.
fields.no_authentication: No device-to-host cryptographic authentication at the protocol layer.
fields.no_access_control: No per-region access control / protection keys at the protocol layer; access control is a host/SoC responsibility.
fields.rowhammer_class_vulnerabilities: DRAM is subject to row-hammer-class disturbance; HBM3's mandatory Refresh-Management (RFM) and adaptive refresh are the standard's mitigation, complementing host-level mitigations.
fields.comparison_to_sibling_standards: Like DDR/LPDDR DRAM, HBM3 leaves confidentiality and authentication to the host; HBM3 strengthens the integrity/reliability side (on-die + link ECC, parity, RFM, RAS) relative to HBM2/HBM2E for data-center use.
fields.notes: The load-bearing security posture for HBM3 is integrity and reliability (ECC, parity, RFM, RAS), not confidentiality/authentication. Memory encryption and access control belong to the host SoC.
